passage:
The robotics lab at the engineering college smelled of solder. The team had just won second place at the state contest, and Professor Nair asked each of the four members to write, privately, what share of the work they had done.

Pradeep wrote 50%. He'd built the arm. Bhupen wrote 45%. He'd written the code. The other two wrote 40% and 35%.

The professor added them up on the whiteboard. "One hundred and seventy percent. Interesting robot."

Everyone laughed, a bit awkwardly. Pradeep felt a flash of annoyance. Surely his share was obvious? Then he remembered the nights Bhupen had stayed till two debugging, which Pradeep had been asleep for.

"You each remember your own late nights very clearly," the professor said. "Other people's, less so."

For the next project, she handed them a shared logbook. "Write what you did, every day. Then we'll talk about credit."

qa.q: What did the four shares add up to?
qa.a: One hundred and seventy percent.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when the total went on the board?
qa.a: Pradeep felt a flash of annoyance, sure his share was obvious, then a little sheepish remembering Bhupen's late nights.

qa.q: Why is the professor's shared logbook a good fix?
qa.a: A written daily record shows everyone's work, not just what each person remembers of their own, so credit is fairer.

qa.q: How might Bhupen see Pradeep's 50%?
qa.a: Bhupen may feel his debugging nights were overlooked, since his own memory of that work is vivid too.

grounding: Each member of a college robotics team thinks he did most of the work, and the shares add up to far more than the whole.

Dear Raghav,

I've been thinking about the argument after our marketing project presentation, and I owe you a proper message.

When the professor asked who led the project, I said I did. You looked hurt. I was annoyed that you looked hurt. In my head, I'd done most of it: the research, the slides, the late calls.

Then last night I went back through our chat history, from week one. You'd drafted the survey. You'd done all the data cleaning. You'd fixed my slides twice at midnight. I honestly didn't remember most of it.

I remembered my work because I was tired while doing it. Yours happened while I was asleep or busy.

I think if we'd both written down what we did each week, neither of us would have been so sure. Can we do that for the next project? And I'm sorry.

Eshaan

qa.a: You'd fixed my slides twice at midnight.

You asked why our hackathon team split up, Gautam? I'm Yusuf. Let me tell you what I learned.

We were three: me, Dev and Kunal. We built a bus-tracking app in thirty-six hours and won. On the train home, someone asked who did most of it. I said, "Honestly, I did about half." Dev said he'd done half. Kunal said he'd done half.

That's a hundred and fifty percent.

We argued all the way to Pune. Each of us could list everything we'd done in detail. I remembered every bug I fixed. I barely remembered Kunal's design work, though it was the reason the judges liked it.

We stopped talking for a month.

Now, on every team, I keep a shared sheet from day one: who did what, each day. It's boring. But when credit comes, nobody has to argue from memory.

The Diwali sales campaign had beaten every target, and in the Monday meeting the director turned to Maria. "Brilliant work. Tell us how you did it."

Maria felt the pull to take all of it. It would have been easy.

Instead she said, "Three things went right, and one went wrong. My part was the idea for the regional videos; I'm proud of that. But we were also lucky: a competitor's launch got delayed, which gave us two clear weeks. And Damini's data team found the timing insight that made the whole thing work. Without her analysis, we'd have launched on the wrong day."

The director looked at Damini, who blushed.

"And what went wrong?" he asked.

"I underestimated the Hindi voice-overs. We were four days late on those. Next time I'll start them first."

After the meeting, Damini caught up with her. "You didn't have to say that about me."

"I did. It was true."

qa.a: We were four days late on those.

qa.q: How did Damini feel when Maria credited her analysis?
qa.a: Damini felt surprised and touched, blushing and later telling Maria she didn't have to say it.

qa.q: What makes Maria's way of taking credit a good example?
qa.a: Maria named her own work, the lucky delay, Damini's key insight and her own mistake, which builds trust and shows what to learn.

qa.q: How might the director see Maria after this meeting?
qa.a: The director likely trusts Maria more, since she gave an honest picture instead of claiming everything.

I'm Rashmi. Last month our team at the architecture firm won a design award for the new library in Kochi. At the ceremony, they called my name first, as project lead.

I had a speech ready that thanked "the team" in one line. Then, backstage, I crossed it out.

What I actually said was this. The core layout was my idea, and I'm proud of it. We were lucky: the site had old trees that gave the building its shape, and that was nature, not me. Wasim solved the ventilation problem that I had got completely wrong in the first draft. Without him, the reading hall would have been an oven.

People clapped. Wasim looked at the floor, then smiled.

Afterwards, my boss said, "That's the first speech I've heard that sounded true."

I think naming the luck and my mistake made people believe the credit I did take.

The board exam was the next morning, the power had gone off in the Nagpur flat, and Madhav was trying to revise by torchlight when his mother, Urmila, came in for the third time. "Have you finished physics?"

"Stop checking on me!" he shouted.

She shouted back. "Don't speak to me like that!"

He slammed the book shut. In his head: I'm stressed, I have an exam, she's controlling me.

In the kitchen, Urmila leaned on the counter, shaking. In her head: I'm scared for him, the power's gone, he's being disrespectful.

Madhav came out an hour later for water. She was sitting in the dark.

"I shouted because I was stressed," he said.

"I shouted because I was worried," she said. "Not to control you."

He blinked. He had thought her shouting was just anger. She had thought his was just rudeness.

They sat together until the lights came back.

"Lucas failed last week."

In Aizawl, the hill roads are steep and wet most of the year. Lalremsiami, sixteen, had started riding her cousin's scooter to tuition without a helmet. "It's only five minutes," she told her uncle Jagdish when he saw her.

"Five minutes is enough," he said.

"Nothing will happen. I'm careful."

On Thursday, a car came round the bend too fast. Lalremsiami braked hard, skidded, and stopped inches from the drain. Her knee was scraped. Her head was fine, but only by luck.

That evening Jagdish sat with her on the steps. He didn't shout. "Everyone your age feels like nothing bad will happen. Your brain is built to think the ride matters more than the risk. That's normal. But the road doesn't care how careful you are."

Her hands were still shaking. She nodded.

The next morning, he left his old helmet on her scooter seat. She wore it.

qa.q: Where did Lalremsiami stop after skidding?
qa.a: Inches from the drain.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami believe nothing would happen without a helmet?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt confident and safe, believing that being careful meant accidents happen to other people.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do after the skid, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Jagdish talked calmly instead of shouting, explained why teens feel invincible, and left her a helmet the next morning.

qa.q: How did Jagdish seem to feel when he first saw her riding without a helmet?
qa.a: Jagdish seemed worried, warning her that five minutes is enough for an accident.

passage:
I'm Ira. Last year, my friend Naveen and I rode his bike to the lake almost every evening. Neither of us wore helmets. We thought helmets were for old people and bad riders.

Naveen's mum used to say, "One day something will happen." We laughed. Nothing ever happened to us.

Then one evening in March, a dog ran across the road. Naveen swerved. We both fell. I scraped my arms. Naveen hit his head on the kerb.

He was okay, eventually. A few stitches, a week at home. But the doctor said a helmet would have saved him from most of it.

I kept thinking: we were so sure it wouldn't be us. It always felt like other people's story.

Now I wear a helmet every time, even for five minutes. And when my younger cousin says, "I'm careful, I'll be fine," I tell her about the dog.

qa.q: What ran across the road?
qa.a: A dog ran across the road.

qa.q: Why did Ira and Naveen not wear helmets?
qa.a: They felt overconfident and safe, sure accidents only happened to old people and bad riders, not to them.

qa.q: What does Ira do now, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Ira wears a helmet every time and tells the younger cousin about the dog, turning the lesson into protection for others.

qa.a: Naveen's mum was probably frightened and upset, having warned them many times.

grounding: A teenager recalls riding without a helmet believing harm was for others, until a friend was hurt in a fall.

In the university placement office, Zeenat had already accepted the offer from a new start-up. "It's going to be amazing," she told her friend Irawati. "They're growing so fast. I'll be a team lead in a year."

"Did you apply anywhere else?"

"Why? This is perfect."

"What if the start-up doesn't do well?"

"It will. I can feel it."

Irawati hesitated. "And the savings? You said you'd move out of your parents' place in three months."

"I'll have a good salary. It'll work out."

Zeenat didn't have a backup offer, or any savings, or a plan if things went wrong. She was so full of hope that planning for trouble felt like jinxing it.

Six months later, the start-up cut half its staff. Zeenat was one of them. She sat in the same placement office, stunned. "I never even thought about this," she said quietly.

qa.a: I'll be a team lead in a year.

Dear Jagdish mama,

You asked how the first year after college went. I'll be honest, since you always are with me.

I was sure everything would go well. The job in Gurugram, the flat with friends, maybe getting engaged by the end of the year. I didn't think about what could go wrong. When you asked about a backup plan at my graduation, I laughed.

In March, the company shut my team down. The flat lease was in my name. And the relationship ended around the same time.

I didn't have a plan for any of it. I felt like I'd been knocked flat.

I'm okay now. I've found another job. But I've learned something. I still hope for good things. I just also ask, "What if it doesn't?" and write down one small backup for each. And I've started talking to a financial adviser at work about planning.

Thank you for asking, back then.

Anand

You want to know what I'd tell my younger self, Baljeet? Okay. I'm Mehak, and at twenty-one I was the most optimistic person you'd ever meet.

I got into a design firm in Mumbai. I was sure I'd be promoted in a year, save enough for my own flat by twenty-five, and my relationship would last forever. Other people had problems. Not me.

I didn't apply anywhere else. I didn't keep any money aside. I didn't even think about what I'd do if the firm struggled.

Then the firm lost its biggest client. Salaries were delayed three months. I had to borrow from my parents. And my relationship, well, that ended too.

I'm not saying don't hope. Hope got me through. But hope with no backup is like a kite with no string. One strong wind, and it's gone.

Now I hope, and I plan. Both.

passage:
Project supervisor's note, new product launch

Shreya is leading her first launch, a healthy snack line for schools. She is clearly hopeful: she talks about it with real energy and believes it will do well. I like that.

What impressed me more was her plan. She has built in a three-week buffer on the timeline, because, as she put it, "Something always goes wrong with packaging." She has kept part of the budget aside for surprises, after checking with finance about how much. And she has a plan B: if schools don't sign up in the first month, she'll test the product in two local shops.

When I asked whether all that planning dampens her optimism, she said, "No. It lets me be optimistic without panicking. If something goes wrong, it's the plan that bends, not me."

I've recommended her approach to the other project leads.

Eshaan

qa.q: How long a buffer did Shreya build into the timeline?
qa.a: A three-week buffer on the timeline.

qa.q: How does Shreya seem to feel about the launch?
qa.a: Shreya seems hopeful and energetic, but also calm, because her buffer and plan B keep her from panicking.

qa.q: What does Shreya's planning do well?
qa.a: It keeps optimism for effort while adding a buffer, reserved budget and plan B, so setbacks bend the plan instead of shaking her.

Sunday night

Signed the offer today! I'm moving to Bengaluru next month to join the start-up. I'm so excited I can barely sleep.

But I'm also doing the boring stuff. Ankita laughed at me today because I made a list.

1. Keep some savings aside, untouched, for emergencies. Asked Abbu's CA friend how to think about it.
2. Ask the start-up to put the offer terms in writing.
3. Keep in touch with two other companies that interviewed me, just in case.
4. Give myself three extra weeks to settle in before expecting to love it.

Ankita said, "Aren't you optimistic?" I am! I really believe it will be great.

But if something goes wrong, I want it to be a bump in the plan, not a crash in me.

Hope, but ready. That's the plan.

Nazia
